entry.description: Reads similes and idioms as literal events.
entry.childHint: Figures of speech are not facts. Ask what the words are really saying.
entry.approvalNote: Cleared on the printed review pack; returned marked up.

textProvenance.note: Ruled when written; absent from the store until now (R403/R410).
textProvenance.authority: annie-seventyseventh-return.md, read from the file, sha256 1c7070f52f67c5d9664f26f1fdefa17323ff1b9111a84ca7c4d093c8c48f79a7

stem.text: Read lines 14 to 15. Where did the Mole find himself when his snout came out into the sunlight?

carriers.key: Rolling in the warm grass of a great meadow.

options.value: On the bank of the river.
At the gap in the hedge.
In a boat painted blue and white.
Rolling in the warm grass of a great meadow.
On a gravelled carriage-drive.
options.execution: Line 10 uses the carriage-drive as a comparison for his tunnel. This takes the comparison as the place he arrives.

stem.text: Read line 18. What does 'the carol of happy birds' mean?

options.value: A Christmas song the birds had learned.
The singing of the birds.
A church bell ringing far away.
The sound of the river chattering.
A shout from someone in the meadow.
options.execution: Line 19 says the singing fell 'almost like a shout'. This takes the comparison as the thing itself.

stem.text: Read lines 22 to 23. What did the elderly rabbit at the gap want from the Mole?

carriers.key: Sixpence for using the private road.

options.value: Sixpence for using the private road.
Help with his own spring-cleaning.
A ride across the river in a boat.
To be let past the hedge himself.
Some onion sauce for his dinner.
options.execution: 'Onion-sauce!' at line 25 is the Mole's jeer on the way past, taken as an order for the rabbit's dinner.

stem.text: The writer calls the river an animal that chases, chuckles and grips things. Read lines 29 to 33. Why does he do this?

carriers.key: To make the river seem alive, playful and always moving.

options.value: To make the river seem alive, playful and always moving.
Because a real animal was swimming in the water.
options.execution: Takes the animal comparison at line 30 as a real animal swimming in the water.

options.value: Because the river was dangerous and might grab the Mole.
Because the Water Rat lived in the bank beside it.
Because the Mole thought a big animal was in front of him.

stem.text: Read lines 33 to 36. The Mole 'trotted as one trots, when very small, by the side of a man who holds one spell-bound by exciting stories'. What does this tell you about the Mole?

carriers.key: The river held the Mole's interest so much that he kept following it.

options.value: The Mole could not keep up with the river.
The Mole was much younger than the Water Rat.
The Mole was looking for a man to help him.
options.execution: Takes the man in the comparison at line 35 as a man the Mole is actually looking for.

options.value: The river held the Mole's interest so much that he kept following it.
The Mole was tired and wanted to go home.

stem.text: Read lines 43 to 45. What did the Mole first notice in the dark hole in the bank?

carriers.key: Something bright and small that twinkled.

options.value: A brown little face with whiskers.
Something bright and small that twinkled.
A tiny star shining in the hole.
options.execution: Line 44 says 'like a tiny star'. This takes the comparison as the thing.

options.value: A glow-worm.
Small neat ears and thick silky hair.

stem.text: The animals act like people, but we never forget they are animals. How does the writer do this?

carriers.key: He gives them houses, money and boats, but keeps their fur, paws and whiskers.

options.value: He keeps the animals quiet, still and dull, but lets the river chatter, gurgle and laugh.
He gives them human names, and leaves the animal ones behind.
He tells the reader, plainly and often, that these animals are really people.
options.execution: Takes the human behaviour as the narrator telling the reader they are people. He never says it anywhere, plainly or otherwise.

options.value: He gives them houses, money and boats, but keeps their fur, paws and whiskers.
He makes every animal speak, move and think in exactly the same way.

stem.text: Read lines 29 to 31. Line 30 says the task was harder than 'bearding a lion in its den'. Why does the writer compare it to that?

carriers.key: To show how frightening an everyday task felt to shy Matthew.

options.value: To show that Matthew is bold, like a lion hunter.
To show that Matthew felt sad about the mistake.
To show how frightening an everyday task felt to shy Matthew.
To show that Matthew had once faced real danger.
options.execution: Reads the comparison as something that happened rather than a picture of a feeling.

stem.text: Read lines 64 to 70. What do these lines show about the three children?

carriers.key: All three reached the same idea without saying anything.

options.value: They wrote the question and the answer in a book.
options.execution: Lines 67 and 68 say the thought was LIKE a school book, so nothing was written.

options.value: All three reached the same idea without saying anything.
They had agreed on the plan earlier in the day.
Mother suggested that they go down to the railway.

stem.text: Read lines 26 to 30, then lines 71 to 73. Why could the morning search never find the garden?

carriers.key: They searched round the house, but the garden lay behind the stables.

options.value: The house stood in a field, and no garden lay near it.
They had seen no wall at all, but only imagined it in the dark.
They searched round the house, but the garden lay behind the stables.
The garden had hidden itself away, and the high wall kept it out of sight.
options.execution: Line 72's hidden itself is a way of speaking, not something the garden did.

stem.text: Read lines 18 to 23. What lies in the mud below the wall?

carriers.key: A boat with its ribs showing, and a gull on it.

options.value: A boat with its ribs showing, and a gull on it.
A half mile of black posts leaning into the channel.
What is left of an old bridge across the channel.
options.execution: Line 22 says the posts are LIKE the last of a bridge; no bridge is stated.

options.value: The remains of a row of four cottages.

stem.text: Read lines 47 to 49. What does Mr Otis's answer show?

carriers.key: He treats her fainting as a cost to be charged for.

options.value: He is worried about the old woman's health.
He wants her to pay for something that she has broken.
options.execution: Line 48 says like breakages, so the breakages are a comparison, not a fact.

options.value: He treats her fainting as a cost to be charged for.
He means to send for a doctor from the nearby village.

stem.text: Look at lines 68 to 70. What did the flame do as the ghost came in?

carriers.key: It leaped up and then fell back again.

options.value: It came on through the heavy door.
It leaped up and then fell back again.
It called out that it knew Marley.
options.execution: Line 70 says as though it cried, so the flame is given a voice it does not have.

options.value: Scrooge changed colour as the thing passed.

stem.text: Look at lines 30 to 34. What was on the top of the rise?

carriers.key: A soldier on a horse watching the road.

options.value: A steep curve of heath-clad land.
A soldier on a horse watching the road.
A stone statue set up on a pedestal.
options.execution: Line 32 says hard and clear LIKE a statue, so the statue is a comparison.

options.value: A stone marker left there by the family.

stem.text: Look at lines 37 and 38. What does "suppress" on line 38 mean here?

carriers.key: To hold back a thing that is coming out.

options.value: To put down a rising by force.
To hold back a thing that is coming out.
To sit quietly at the table.
To press down hard on a thing.
options.execution: Built out of press, which sits inside the word.

stem.text: Look at lines 76 to 78. What does "scruples" on line 77 mean here?

carriers.key: Uneasy feelings about whether a thing is right.

options.value: Very small weights used by a chemist.
The value of the money they have staked.
Careful scraping away at a surface.
options.execution: Built from the scrape the word sounds like.

options.value: Uneasy feelings about whether a thing is right.
